strengths: SFTMix addresses a relevant NLP problem with a concrete recipe: partition instruction-tuning data using training dynamics, interpolate token representations and targets, and add a Mixup loss. Applying this approach does not require additional human annotation or proprietary-model scoring.

The empirical coverage is substantial. Table 1 reports improvements across seven model–dataset combinations spanning three model families. Healthcare experiments provide complementary evidence, increasing average accuracy from 60.72% to 62.05% for Llama and from 54.32% to 55.98% for Mistral.

Human evaluation supports the automated results: across 200 judgments covering 80 instructions, SFTMix receives 42.5% wins versus 26.5% for NTP, with 31% ties. Reporting length-controlled AlpacaEval scores also addresses an important evaluator bias.

Experiments with LoRA, data selection, a smaller reference model, and alternative regularization weights provide useful evidence about the recipe’s applicability. Transferring the default hyperparameters across multiple settings strengthens the empirical contribution.
weaknesses: The central claim that confidence-based pairing is crucial is not isolated experimentally. There is no unrestricted random-pair Mixup baseline on the same data, nor a comparison against pairing within confidence groups. Section 5.2 changes the response dataset and does not include confidence-based SFTMix on that modified dataset. Consequently, its results cannot establish the necessity of training-dynamics-based pairing. This missing control, together with the evaluation and reproducibility concerns, prevents a clear Findings recommendation.

The proposed mechanism exceeds the supporting evidence. Separation of extreme-confidence examples in t-SNE and a 7% reduction in training-confidence standard deviation do not establish reduced overfitting on confident examples or improved generalization on unconfident examples. Held-out measurements for the respective groups are needed. Section 3.4 establishes that Mixup changes the gradient, without explaining why confidence-based pairing improves generalization.

Evaluation uncertainty and model selection are insufficiently addressed. The paper averages repeated evaluations but provides no confidence intervals or variation across independently trained seeds, despite several modest improvements. Appendix A.1 selects hyperparameters using MT-Bench and AlpacaEval-2, which also supply the main reported results; no separate validation protocol is described. Transfer results on other settings are encouraging, but the tuned setting needs an independent assessment.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite the useful optimizer and epoch details. The manuscript does not link an implementation or specify important settings such as confidence-checkpoint locations, input templates, maximum sequence length, exact generation and judge configurations, and LoRA parameters. The human evaluation also lacks annotator counts, assignment procedures, and agreement measurements.

The broader comparative and practical advantages remain uncertain. Closely related cartography-based Mixup work is cited without a sufficiently explicit account of the methodological advance. Comparisons with simple regularizers such as NEFTune would help establish added value. The reference-model training and checkpoint-scoring costs are acknowledged but not quantified, and no comparison at matched total compute is provided.

Several technical explanations need correction. The loss definitions negate cross-entropy H, whereas Section 3.4 uses the gradient of positive cross-entropy. Appendix A.1 incorrectly describes Beta(0.1, 0.1) as flat and producing mixtures far from the endpoints. Section 5.3’s distinction between an additional loss and regularization is a change in its coefficient, rather than a separate objective construction.
